intro: A classifier assigns scores, but a downstream system must decide which items to flag. Move the decision threshold and inspect the mistakes rather than relying on accuracy alone.
task: Return a dictionary with tp, fp, tn, fn, precision, recall, and f1. Predict positive when score >= threshold, including exact ties.
requirements: y and scores are nonempty one-dimensional arrays of equal length. y contains only 0 or 1; scores and threshold lie in [0,1].
Reject incompatible shapes, non-finite values, invalid labels, and a non-scalar threshold with ValueError.
Return numeric counts and metrics. Use zero when a precision, recall, or F1 denominator is zero.
Compute counts before ratios. Do not modify inputs. Scores are supplied probabilities; this task does not fit or calibrate a classifier.

examples.name: Mixed decisions
examples.output: {tp:1, fp:1, tn:1, fn:1, precision:0.5, recall:0.5, f1:0.5}

examples.name: Threshold ties are positive
examples.output: {tp:1, fp:1, tn:0, fn:0, precision:0.5, recall:1, f1:0.666667}

examples.name: No predicted positives
examples.output: {tp:0, fp:0, tn:1, fn:1, precision:0, recall:0, f1:0}

hints.title: Make two masks
hints.body: Compare scores with threshold and compare y with 1. Their intersections identify the four count categories.

hints.title: Ask which denominator
hints.body: Precision asks how many flagged items are positive. Recall asks how many actual positives were flagged.

hints.title: Handle an empty denominator
hints.body: Use the documented zero convention. F1 can be computed directly as 2*tp/(2*tp+fp+fn).

explanation: The threshold is a decision rule layered on top of the score. With the same scores, reducing it cannot remove a predicted positive; both true-positive and false-positive counts can increase.
Precision divides true positives by all predicted positives. Recall divides true positives by all actual positives. F1 balances these ratios but does not encode the real cost of either mistake.

Choose and compare thresholds on validation data using the application's costs, then evaluate the chosen procedure on held-out data. This small example does not establish that a threshold is appropriate for a real deployment.
Try thresholds 0.3, 0.5, and 0.85 on the first example. Which errors change? Explain why a score of 0.8 is not automatically a trustworthy 80% probability without calibration evidence.
formula: precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN)
